 1   I.     INTRODUCTION

 2          Plaintiff’s opposition brief defends this lawsuit only by distorting the governing pleading

 3   standard, mischaracterizing the Complaint, and outright ignoring many of PHH’s grounds for

 4   dismissal. None of that cures the fundamental flaw in his pleadings: Plaintiff contractually

 5   authorized the alleged information sharing at issue. Nor does Plaintiff’s obfuscation save the claims

 6   from their various other legal shortcomings. The Court should dismiss with prejudice.

 7   II.    ARGUMENT

 8          A.      Plaintiff’s Claims Fail As A Matter Of Law Because He Consented.

 9          Plaintiff defends his claims by disputing his own contractual consent. But that tactic

10   demonstrates a basic misunderstanding of the pleading standard. His brief spends several pages

11   insisting that “the court must presume” he never consented to PHH’s information sharing simply

12   because the Complaint says, in conclusory fashion, that he “did not consent.” Opp. 4-5; see id. at 7

13   (“a reasonable consumer would not have understood PHH’s policy as providing consent for these

14   activities”). But those assertions are entitled to no weight. They should first be rejected because

15   they contradict his admission that he entered into the Privacy Contracts, which specifically disclose

16   the challenged activities. See Compl. ¶¶ 90, 135, Exs. A–D. Such “contradictory allegations … are

17   inherently implausible.” Hernandez v. Select Portfolio, Inc., 2015 WL 3914741, at *10 (C.D. Cal.

18   2015); see also Sprewell v. Golden State Warriors, 266 F.3d 979, 988 (9th Cir. 2001) (courts “need

19   not … accept as true allegations that contradict” exhibits). Moreover, the assertions are

20   quintessential “legal conclusions couched as factual allegations” and are not “sufficient” to state a

21   claim. Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544, 555 (2007). That is why courts have set aside

22   nearly identical assertions when dismissing claims on consent grounds. See, e.g., M.D. v. Google

23   LLC, 2025 WL 2710095, at *4 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 23, 2025) (dismissing even though “Plaintiffs allege

24   they did not consent to Defendant’s interception of their personal information”); Lakes v. Ubisoft,

25   Inc., 777 F. Supp. 3d 1047, 1051 (N.D. Cal. 2025) (dismissing claims even though “Plaintiffs

26   allege” defendant shared information “without obtaining their consent”). The existence of consent

27   rises or falls solely on the “factual content” pled. Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009)

28   (emphasis added).
